newsitem.title: USA: FTC OKs Pratt, General Electric venture.
newsitem.headline: FTC OKs Pratt, General Electric venture.

text.p: A joint venture between Pratt & Whitney and General Electric Co to build engines for Boeing Co's longer-range 747s has been approved by the Federal Trade Commission, Pratt's top executive said Tuesday.
The FTC approved the venture in late November but no announcement was made at the time, Pratt President Karl Krapek told Reuters in an interview.
"The partnership is working out great so far," Krapek said.
"All the milestones are being met, and our engine is on the original target," said Krapek. "We are plowing ahead and we are not veering off our schedule."
The Pratt-GE venture also needs approval from European trade authorities, but Krapek said he expected their go-ahead "by early spring at the latest."
Pratt & Whitney is a unit of United Technologies Corp .
Flight tests for the 747-500/600s, which can carry up to 550 passengers, are expected to start by the end of 1999.
"Boeing has our pricing," said Krapek. "There's at least five customers that have had our initial proposals on the engine, in detail. We've been out actively selling."
Krapek said the potential customers were "the big guys" but did not identify them.
The 50-50 engine partnership between GE and Pratt, announced in May of this year, will cost both companies a combined $750-$800 million over four years, ending in 1999, he said.
Industry analysts expect fierce competition between GE-Pratt and Rolls-Royce Ltd to develop the new engine.
But the development race is not a "winner take all" affair, because each airline that buys a longer-range 747 will get to choose its own engine supplier.
"Obviously, we rank this project as a top priority," said Krapek. "Since we have number one market share in the 747s, we need to serve those customers as they move up."
Asked about the pricing of the new engine, Krapek said: "The cost target is, we want an engine in this thrust class to cost less than current engines with 20,000 pounds less thrust."
"In other words, if it's an 80,000-pound thrust bearing engine, we want it to cost less than today's current 60,000-pound thrust engine."
